title: The father's order
hookLine: a father's terrible order: two sons refuse, and one obeys
carry: honor parents as god, and dharma is subtle
tomorrow: a king takes the family's cow. what does the son with the axe do?
last: A FORM THAT WON'T STAY IN ONE BOX.

cards: Every family has an argument people are still having at the dinner table years later. The tradition has this one.

It's a hard story, and the Bhagavata tells it plainly; it may be one to hear first before sharing it with a child. Renuka goes to the river for water, lingers watching a heavenly king at play, and comes home late.
Her husband, Jamadagni, knows why, and in his anger he orders his sons to kill her. The older brothers refuse. Parashurama obeys.

teach.h: THE WISH: BACK, WITH NO MEMORY.
teach.b: His father, pleased, offers him a wish. And Parashurama asks for his mother and brothers to live again, with no memory of what happened. Jamadagni grants it, and they rise as if waking from sleep.
So who did right? Here's the first view, at its strongest. The Bhagavata says Parashurama obeyed because he knew his father's power, the strength built up by long discipline.

teach.h: VIEW ONE: HE TRUSTED HIS FATHER.
teach.b: He trusted that what his father could order, his father could undo. And when he was offered anything at all, he spent it on undoing the harm and sparing his family the memory.
Obedience, in this reading, is trust in someone who sees further than you. Now the second view, at its strongest. The older brothers refused, and some readers take their side.
An old line in the Taittiriya Upanishad tells a student: let your mother be a god to you; let your father be a god to you.

teach.h: VIEW TWO: THE MOTHER COMES FIRST.
teach.b: The mother comes first in that line. No order, these readers say, not even a father's, can make harming her right, and the brothers saw it. The tradition hasn't closed this argument.
The Mahabharata has a phrase for days like this: dharma is subtle. Honoring your parents as gods is a real Hindu duty; knowing what it asks of you on the worst day is the hard part.

how: Renuka is honored in her own right in parts of India, where temples to her as a goddess, Renuka Devi or Yellamma, keep her story alive alongside her son's.

games.q: a classmate says Hindus just do whatever their parents say. after today's story, what's the fairest answer?
o: parents are honored like gods, and the tradition still argues about where obedience ends.
true; obeying your parents is the whole teaching.
not really; Hindus don't put much weight on parents.
games.why: let your mother be a god to you, let your father be a god to you: real honor. and the story keeps two refusing brothers beside the son who obeyed. dharma is subtle.

practice: If you have paper, write one line for the side you'd take, and one line for the other side, the strongest you can make it. Or just form the two sentences in your mind.
Then sit with both, and let neither one win for the length of the sit.

wordCard.voice: Parashurama: the sage's son with the axe, who obeyed a terrible order and spent his wish on undoing it.

orig.note: Sanskrit, from the Taittiriya Upanishad: let your mother be a god to you. The line names the mother first.

carryVoice: Hold on to it: honor your parents as god, and dharma is subtle. One son obeyed; two refused. Day fifteen-fifty, done.
